paragraphs: Remote sensing instruments provide different views of the same geographic scene, but some observations are often missing. Training a separate translator for every pair of sensing modalities becomes increasingly expensive as modalities are added. Any2Any instead treats translation as recovering a shared scene representation from whichever observations are available.

The framework uses latent diffusion and maps heterogeneous inputs into a geometrically aligned representation space. A shared backbone learns semantic mappings, while modality-specific representation learning handles differences between input types. Small adapters associated with each target modality correct systematic mismatches in this space without increasing inference complexity. This arrangement lets translation tasks share a common model rather than requiring independent pairwise systems.

The authors also introduce RST-1M, a million-scale dataset covering five sensing modalities. Its paired observations provide anchors for learning from supervision that is sparse but connected. Across 14 translation tasks, Any2Any consistently outperforms pairwise methods and generalizes strongly to previously unseen modality pairs. These findings support shared scene representations as a useful basis for translation when complete observations are unavailable.
icml-2026-any2any-unified-arbitrary-moda.tldr: Any2Any shares a latent scene representation across remote sensing modalities, improving translation and generalization to unseen modality pairs.

paragraphs: Compressing a multimodal language model requires transferring both visual understanding and coherent generation to a smaller model. The paper argues that matching a teacher’s next-token predictions alone overlooks important relationships between tokens. Align-TI therefore organizes distillation around how instructions interact with visual information and how response tokens interact during generation.

Its first component, IVA, trains the student to match the teacher’s attention to salient visual regions relevant to the instruction. The aim is to transfer the ability to extract the right information from an image. Its second component, TPA, aligns sequential token-to-token transition probabilities, giving the student a training signal about the teacher’s evolving generation behavior. Together, these components address information selection and response construction.

The reported experiments show a 2.6% relative improvement over Vanilla KD. The distilled Align-TI-2B also outperforms the larger LLaVA-1.5-7B by a reported 7.0%. These comparisons support the value of transferring token interactions for efficient multimodal models, beyond simply reproducing isolated next-token outputs.
icml-2026-beyond-next-token-alignment-di.tldr: Align-TI distills multimodal models by transferring instruction-relevant visual interactions and response-token transitions.

paragraphs: Native GUI agents interpret screenshots and act directly on digital interfaces using a vision-language model. Although these agents have improved on general interface tasks, interactive CAPTCHAs remain difficult. Specialized CAPTCHA systems address those challenges but do not provide the broader capabilities of a general GUI agent. ReCAP aims to combine both abilities within one native agent.

The authors build a dynamic environment covering seven representative CAPTCHA types and an automated pipeline for collecting and curating interaction trajectories. These trajectories pair actions with reasoning traces, giving training examples that connect visual interpretation, decisions, and interface interaction. The environment is designed to exercise different primitive and complementary capabilities needed for CAPTCHA solving.

ReCAP also learns from unsuccessful attempts. Failed trajectories become self-correction examples that teach the agent to reflect on intermediate errors and adjust its actions during an ongoing interaction. On synthetic and real-world test sets, the resulting agents substantially improve CAPTCHA success over their base models while retaining strong general GUI benchmark performance. The findings support training recovery behavior alongside successful action sequences.
icml-2026-captcha-solving-for-native-gui.tldr: ReCAP uses automated interaction data and failed-attempt training to improve CAPTCHA solving while retaining general GUI abilities.

paragraphs: Singular value decomposition can compress language-model weight matrices into smaller low-rank representations without retraining. A central choice is how much capacity to retain in each part of the model. CGSVD challenges uniform allocation because different layers and components need not contain equal amounts of redundancy or contribute equally to preserving representations.

The method distributes retained capacity at two levels. Angular distance measures significance across layers, while spectral entropy assesses compressibility within layers. These signals guide where compression should be more or less aggressive. Because matrix ranks must be integers, the initial allocation can miss the requested total parameter budget. An Iterative Residual Filling mechanism adjusts the allocation to meet the global compression target precisely.

Experiments cover language-model families with 3B to 13B parameters. At a reported 30% compression ratio for LLaMA3.1-8B, CGSVD improves average zero-shot accuracy by 6.08% and lowers perplexity by 15.46 compared with the baseline. The findings support allocating compression unevenly according to measured model structure, rather than treating all components as equally expendable.
icml-2026-cgsvd-cascaded-granular-singul.tldr: CGSVD compresses language models without retraining by allocating low-rank capacity according to layer importance and component compressibility.

paragraphs: Sampling molecular configurations at equilibrium is difficult because the desired distribution must reflect the system’s physical behavior. Boltzmann Generators combine generative models with importance sampling, but their practical scalability is limited. Coarse-grained representations reduce the number of coordinates being modeled, making larger systems more manageable, yet often lack the reweighting needed for asymptotically correct statistics.

Coarse-Grained Boltzmann Generators bring generation and importance sampling into this reduced coordinate space. A flow-based model produces configurations, and a learned potential of mean force supplies the basis for reweighting them. This potential describes the effective behavior relevant to the coarse-grained representation. The authors show that it can be learned from rapidly converged trajectories using enhanced sampling force matching.

Experiments show that the method captures interactions mediated by solvent even in highly reduced representations. It also substantially lowers computational cost relative to atomistic Boltzmann Generators. The contribution is a framework that combines dimensionality reduction with a reweighting procedure, providing a practical route toward equilibrium sampling for larger molecular systems.
icml-2026-coarse-grained-boltzmann-gener.tldr: Coarse-Grained Boltzmann Generators combine reduced-coordinate generation with learned reweighting to make molecular equilibrium sampling less costly.

paragraphs: Deep search requires navigating information, deciding what to retain, and assembling an answer. The paper argues that assigning all these responsibilities to one agent can create cognitive overload. Splitting the work among agents is an alternative, but systems built from frozen models cannot improve their collaboration by learning from failures.

DECOR formulates deep search as a multi-agent reinforcement learning problem with three functional roles. A Planner directs navigation, a Filter maintains a memory with less noise, and an Answerer synthesizes the result. The agents are optimized together rather than merely connected through a fixed orchestration procedure. Their training combines feedback specific to each role with signals about the team’s final outcome.

This reward structure links local responsibilities to overall success: each agent receives guidance about its own contribution while participating in a shared objective. Experiments across seven benchmarks show significant improvements over strong monolithic baselines. The results support learned functional decomposition as an effective response to cognitive overload in the evaluated deep-search settings.
icml-2026-decor-learning-to-decompose-an.tldr: DECOR jointly trains planning, filtering, and answering agents to improve collaboration and performance in deep search.

paragraphs: Set representation models must summarize collections of elements into useful representations. A model trained on curated sets may encounter outliers or missing components after deployment, distorting that summary and harming performance. This paper focuses on those element-level changes at inference time, rather than assuming deployed inputs will remain as clean as the training data.

SW-DRSO changes the training objective to account for a family of plausible input variations. It optimizes a tractable surrogate for the worst-case expected loss within that family. This asks the model to prepare for adverse variations during learning instead of minimizing errors only on the observed training sets.

Searching directly over corrupted sets is intractable in the proposed formulation, so the method introduces a barycentric adversary. It approximates that search through differentiable optimization over simplex weights, allowing the adversarial component to participate in training. Experiments across four tasks show improved robustness to corruption while maintaining high overall performance. The contribution is a practical training approach for making set representations less vulnerable to changes in their constituent elements.
icml-2026-distributionally-robust-set-re.tldr: SW-DRSO trains set representations against plausible element corruptions using a tractable approximation to worst-case loss.

paragraphs: Training tool-using agents on synthetic tasks does not automatically prepare them for new tasks or unfamiliar tool combinations. DIVE attributes this brittleness to insufficient structural diversity in training data. Its challenge is to increase that diversity while keeping generated tasks executable and verifiable, so that variety does not come at the expense of grounded supervision.

DIVE reverses the synthesis process: it first executes diverse real-world tools, then derives tasks strictly supported by the resulting execution traces. It controls diversity through tool-pool coverage and the variety of tools used within each task. The resulting collection contains 48,000 trajectories across 374 tools and five domains, with 46,398 distinct toolsets and 39,810 distinct tool-call graphs.

Training Qwen3-8B with 48,000 supervised examples and 3,200 reinforcement learning examples improves performance by 22 average points across nine out-of-distribution benchmarks. It also exceeds the strongest 8B baseline by a reported 68%. Controlled experiments under a fixed budget find that increasing diversity consistently beats increasing quantity, even with four times less data.
icml-2026-dive-scaling-diversity-in-agen.tldr: DIVE derives training tasks from real tool executions and finds that structural diversity improves generalization more than data quantity.

paragraphs: Efficient language-model adaptation often treats choosing training examples and choosing trainable parameters as separate problems. This paper investigates whether those decisions are coupled. Its Strong Map Hypothesis proposes that a sparse subset of attention heads dominates adaptation to a particular task and corresponds to specific useful patterns in the data.

The P2D framework uses a lightweight proxy to identify these task-sensitive heads. The same heads then guide both structural pruning and the selection of high-affinity training examples. This gives parameter selection and data selection a shared reference point: the parts of the model most relevant to the task also help determine which examples should be used for adaptation.

The authors introduce an Alignment Efficiency Ratio that accounts for selection latency as well as training time. In their experiments, updating 10% of attention heads using 10% of the data produces an 8.3 percentage-point gain over strong baselines and a 7.0-fold end-to-end speedup. These findings support coordinating parameter and data choices as a practical efficiency strategy, while the proposed attention-head relationship remains framed as a hypothesis.
icml-2026-from-parameters-to-data-a-task.tldr: P2D uses task-sensitive attention heads to coordinate parameter pruning and data selection, improving reported adaptation efficiency and performance.

paragraphs: Federated graph learning lets distributed clients collaborate on graph neural networks while keeping their data private. GraphP-FL addresses two difficulties in that collaboration: local graph connections may be noisy, and alignment with a global model can disrupt knowledge that matters to an individual client. Both can weaken the representations learned locally.

The framework first reconstructs topology dynamically on each client using self-supervision. It mines implicit dependencies to correct noisy connections and reduce the propagation of structural errors. A second component uses Fisher information to assess parameter importance. Its elastic alignment applies different strengths of constraint in different parameter directions, protecting critical local knowledge while allowing flexible alignment with the global model.

The two mechanisms address complementary sources of degradation: unreliable relationships in the input graph and harmful changes during model alignment. Experiments span seven benchmarks, including biochemical molecules, social networks, and large-scale encrypted traffic. GraphP-FL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with reported accuracy improvements of up to 8.6%, alongside stronger generalization and robustness. These findings support combining topology correction with importance-sensitive personalization.
icml-2026-graphp-fl-personalized-federat.tldr: GraphP-FL combines local graph repair with Fisher-based parameter alignment to improve personalized federated graph learning.

paragraphs: Dynamic retrieval-augmented generation relies on a planner to coordinate several steps of information gathering and reasoning. The paper identifies a mismatch when that planner improves but its execution modules remain frozen. A sophisticated plan may demand behavior the executors cannot provide, so adding orchestration complexity can even reduce performance.

JADE jointly optimizes planning and execution within flexible, multi-turn workflows. It represents the system as a cooperative team of agents sharing a backbone and trains the team end to end using rewards based on final outcomes. This enables both sides to adapt: the planner learns what its executors can accomplish, while the executors learn to better carry out the planner’s intentions.

The approach brings joint learning to workflows whose structure can change dynamically. Reported experiments show strong performance improvements from this coordinated optimization. Dynamic orchestration also provides flexibility in balancing efficiency against effectiveness. The findings support treating planning quality and execution capability as interdependent parts of an agentic retrieval system, rather than expecting improvements in either component to translate automatically into better overall results.
icml-2026-jade-bridging-the-strategic-op.tldr: JADE jointly trains planners and executors so dynamic retrieval workflows adapt their strategies and capabilities together.

paragraphs: Continual learning must accommodate new tasks while preserving previously learned knowledge. With LoRA, two low-rank factors interact to produce a full weight update. The paper identifies a problem in that interaction: independently updating the factors can make the combined update violate orthogonality to the subspace representing earlier knowledge, reintroducing interference.

Janus-LoRA addresses this with Gradient Rectification, a closed-form procedure that mathematically decouples the factor updates. It enforces orthogonality against a historical knowledge subspace maintained through efficient online estimation. However, the paper also observes that simply enforcing orthogonality can hinder the ability to learn new tasks, so preserving old parameters is only part of the solution.

A Decoupled Margin Loss adds feature-level separation by pushing new representations away from old ones. This creates distinct regions for new learning with less interference. Experiments on challenging benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance and a stronger balance between retaining knowledge and acquiring new capabilities. The central contribution is coordinating constraints on parameter changes with separation in the learned feature space.
icml-2026-janus-lora-a-balanced-low-rank.tldr: Janus-LoRA combines corrected low-rank updates with feature separation to balance knowledge retention and new learning.

paragraphs: Scientific optimization often involves experiments that are expensive to run and therefore scarce. Language-model predictions are much cheaper, but integrating a model into an optimization pipeline does not by itself exploit that cost difference. LABO makes the choice between inexpensive predictions and costly observations an explicit part of Bayesian optimization.

The framework combines both sources of information in one optimization loop. A gating mechanism dynamically controls how much the search relies on language-model predictions versus actual experiments. Cheap model evaluations explore broadly, while real experiments are reserved for regions with high uncertainty. This allocation aims to extract more useful progress from a limited experimental budget.

The paper provides a cumulative regret bound to formalize the efficiency gain; regret measures the accumulated shortfall of optimization decisions relative to an optimal choice. Across diverse scientific tasks, LABO consistently outperforms existing methods under identical experimental budgets. The empirical result supports the framework’s sample efficiency, while the theoretical analysis gives a formal basis for its strategy of combining broad prediction-based exploration with selective experimentation.
icml-2026-labo-llm-accelerated-bayesian-.tldr: LABO combines cheap language-model predictions with selectively chosen experiments to improve Bayesian optimization under limited experimental budgets.

paragraphs: A benchmark affects more than how models are measured: it also influences what their developers choose to improve. This paper studies providers who can spend post-training resources on benchmark-specific gains, raising observed scores without necessarily changing underlying model quality. The question is whether an evaluation protocol can produce reliable rankings despite these incentives.

The authors model evaluation as a Stackelberg game. A benchmark designer first chooses the protocol, then model providers compete under that choice. Each model has unknown latent quality, and each provider decides how to allocate resources to score improvement. Within this formulation, the authors prove that current benchmarks induce games without a Nash equilibrium among developers.

The paper also establishes a positive result for tune-before-test. Under mild conditions, this protocol induces a unique Nash equilibrium whose ranking follows latent model quality. The absence of equilibrium in the first result offers a possible explanation for opaque strategic behavior; the conditional positive result shows that better-aligned incentives are achievable within the model through evaluation design.
icml-2026-leaderboard-incentives-model-r.tldr: A game-theoretic analysis shows that tune-before-test can, under mild conditions, align strategic model competition with latent-quality rankings.

paragraphs: Security flaws in generated code can arise from a very small decision, even a single token. The paper argues that optimizing entire output sequences can miss these localized mistakes. Tree-like Self-Play reframes secure code generation as a sequence of decisions so that learning can focus on the points where vulnerabilities emerge.

The model explores a branching tree of code trajectories containing both secure paths and vulnerable alternatives. Comparing its own alternatives supplies a dense, on-policy learning signal at critical decision nodes. This structure is intended to teach precise correction of local errors, rather than relying only on an overall judgment of a completed program.

On Python security benchmarks, TSP raises CodeLlama-7B’s SPR@1 pass rate to 75.8%, compared with 57.0% for supervised fine-tuning, and outperforms unstructured self-play baselines. It also reduces vulnerabilities in unseen weakness categories by 24.5% and transfers learning from C/C++ to Python, Go, and JavaScript. These results suggest that the training can capture security principles extending beyond memorized patches and the original training language.
icml-2026-learn-from-your-mistakes-tree-.tldr: Tree-like Self-Play trains code models on branching secure and vulnerable alternatives, improving localized security decisions and cross-language transfer.

paragraphs: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models into one model with multiple capabilities. The weights assigned to those source models influence the result, yet existing approaches often fix these coefficients or tune them manually. MetaMerging instead learns coefficients with a specific downstream goal: creating a shared model that is well suited to task-specific adapter training.

The method uses two nested learning loops. The inner loop simulates adapter updates for downstream tasks. The outer loop adjusts merging coefficients based on that adaptation process. This makes the merge sensitive to how the resulting model will be used, connecting the initial combination of parameters to subsequent task-specific learning.

Experiments in computer vision and natural language processing report strong downstream performance and demonstrate the value of meta-learning compared with other parameter-merging methods. The resulting models are described as more balanced and generalizable. The contribution is an adaptive way to construct a multi-task starting point, with the merging decision evaluated through its usefulness for later adapter training.
icml-2026-learn-to-merge-meta-learning-f.tldr: MetaMerging learns model-merging coefficients by optimizing how well the merged model supports downstream adapter training.

paragraphs: Experimental design can balance measured covariates so that comparison groups are more similar before outcomes are assessed. Classical approaches primarily control linear imbalance. This paper extends that objective to nonlinear functions of covariates, including polynomial structure and more general smooth function classes, allowing the design to address richer patterns in the measured characteristics.

The method builds on the Gram-Schmidt Walk framework and directly controls nonlinear imbalance while retaining sufficient robustness to model misspecification. Its implementation works with a Gram matrix, which represents relationships among observations. This avoids explicitly constructing potentially expensive nonlinear expansions of the covariates, making the richer balancing objective more computationally accessible.

The authors further accelerate the design using a low-rank approximation of the Gram matrix. They report runtimes comparable to the original Gram-Schmidt Walk approach while preserving nonlinear balance and robustness. The contribution is therefore both statistical and computational: it broadens the kinds of covariate structure that experimental design can balance and supplies an implementation intended to keep that broader objective practical.
icml-2026-nonlinear-covariate-balance-in.tldr: This design balances nonlinear covariate structure through Gram matrices while retaining robustness and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Offline learning in a two-player zero-sum Markov game seeks equilibrium strategies using a fixed dataset. Distribution shift makes this difficult because learned strategies may depend on behavior that the data poorly supports. Existing approaches often add explicit pessimism. This paper shows that KL regularization alone can stabilize learning and guarantee convergence under the stated conditions.

The theoretical framework, ROSE, achieves a statistical convergence rate of approximately 1/n, suppressing logarithmic factors, where n is the sample count. This improves on the approximately 1/√n rate described for unregularized settings. The guarantee requires unilateral concentrability and a coupled condition on regularization and the reference policy, so those assumptions are part of the result.

The authors then introduce SOS-MD, a model-free algorithm combining least-squares value estimation with iterative self-play updates. They prove that its final iterate attains the same statistical rate, plus an optimization error that vanishes at approximately 1/√T over T self-play iterations. This connects the framework’s statistical advantage to an implementable learning procedure with an explicit optimization guarantee.
icml-2026-offline-two-player-zero-sum-ma.tldr: Under stated coverage and regularization conditions, KL regularization enables fast equilibrium learning in offline zero-sum Markov games.

paragraphs: Snapshot spectral imaging compresses a three-dimensional hyperspectral scene into a single two-dimensional measurement. Reconstruction methods commonly recover a fixed set of wavelength bands, even though scene spectra are continuous. Phy-CoSF addresses this mismatch by learning a representation that can be queried at target wavelengths rather than producing only a predetermined spectral grid.

The architecture combines deep unfolding networks with implicit neural representations. Its two-phase design connects training at discrete wavelengths to continuous spectral rendering. Within each unfolding stage, a continuous spectral fields module acts as a dynamic prior. Three branches mix spatial, frequency, and channel information, while a synthesis head predicts spectral intensities from continuous wavelength coordinates.

This design supports both reconstruction and spectral super-resolution through the same continuous representation. Experiments demonstrate modeling at arbitrary spectral resolutions and improvements over many state-of-the-art methods in reconstruction fidelity and preservation of spectral detail. The findings support representing wavelength as a continuous query coordinate when recovering spectral information from compressed measurements, while retaining the reconstruction structure supplied by the unfolding network.
icml-2026-phy-cosf-physics-guided-contin.tldr: Phy-CoSF reconstructs hyperspectral images through continuous wavelength queries, enabling flexible spectral resolution from snapshot measurements.

paragraphs: Quantization-aware training prepares language models to operate at reduced numerical precision. This paper studies how the resulting quantization error changes with model size, training-data volume, and quantization group size, especially when both weights and activations use four bits. Its proposed scaling law incorporates factors omitted by earlier laws.

Across 268 experiments, quantization error decreases with larger models but increases with more training tokens and coarser quantization granularity. Separating weight error from activation error reveals similar overall trends with different sensitivities: weight error grows more rapidly as training tokens increase. These findings concern quantization error, so the increase with data should not be read as a general claim that additional training worsens model quality.

The analysis identifies outlier-driven activation error in the FC2 layer as the primary W4A4 bottleneck. Mixed precision targeting that bottleneck brings weight and activation errors to similar levels. With more training data, weight error eventually exceeds activation error. The results therefore point to changing priorities for quantization improvement as the training-data budget grows.
icml-2026-scaling-law-for-quantization-a.tldr: A scaling study links quantization error to model size, training tokens, and group size, identifying shifting weight and activation bottlenecks.

paragraphs: Different questions within the same task can require different expertise, so choosing one expert model for an entire task can be too coarse. Skill-MoE selects existing pretrained models for individual queries. It uses symbolic skill inference and requires no gradient-based training for its expert-selection framework.

For each query, the system infers relevant skills, such as algebra, and selects experts accordingly. Each selected expert generates its own reasoning, after which an aggregator chosen for response integration synthesizes their outputs. To reduce repeated loading and offloading, batch inference groups queries by their assigned experts. Each expert model can then be loaded only once for the grouped work.

This batching enables 16 expert models to run on one GPU with runtime comparable to earlier multi-agent baselines using four GPUs. Across MMLU-Pro, GPQA, AIME, and MedMCQA, Skill-MoE reports an average absolute improvement of 8.15% over the best baseline. It also generalizes well to unseen tasks and outperforms discussion-based approaches without costly multi-round interactions, supporting query-specific routing plus synthesis as an effective combination.
icml-2026-skill-based-mixture-of-experts.tldr: Skill-MoE routes each query to relevant pretrained experts and batches their work to improve reasoning with lower hardware demands.

paragraphs: Medical images can contain only a small amount of visual evidence relevant to a particular question. The authors find that removing visual tokens outside the relevant region improves medical reasoning. ViToS turns that observation into a unified reinforcement learning framework that learns both where to focus and how to answer using the retained visual information.

One shared policy model has two task branches. The grounding branch identifies relevant visual regions, while the reasoning branch answers after visual token pruning. Because these tasks are coupled, their updates can conflict. The proposed cross-feedback sequential optimization coordinates their learning to avoid gradient conflict and facilitate convergence of the shared policy.

Across seven medical benchmarks, ViToS retains 77% of the original visual-token sequence length. It reports relative performance of 108.27% on Lingshu-7B and 104.16% on HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B, together with faster inference. These are relative performance levels, rather than gains of 108% and 104%. The findings support learning visual selection jointly with answering to improve the efficiency of medical multimodal reasoning.
icml-2026-token-sparse-medical-multimoda.tldr: ViToS jointly learns visual grounding and token-pruned medical reasoning, improving reported performance while retaining 77% of visual tokens.

paragraphs: Learning-augmented paging uses predictions to help decide which items a cache should retain. Its robustness guarantee bounds worst-case performance even when those predictions are inaccurate. Earlier randomized methods achieved a bound of 2H_k plus an additive constant, leaving a gap to the optimal competitive ratio H_k, where k denotes cache capacity.

The paper first proves a new property of the latest H_k-competitive online algorithm to support analysis in the prediction-assisted setting. It then introduces the relative prediction budget as a common primitive for understanding robustness. Through this lens, previous algorithms either rely too heavily on predictions or fail to use them fully.

Guided by that analysis, the authors develop a framework with robustness H_k plus an additive constant. This closes the leading-factor gap while retaining an additive difference from the optimum. Experiments also show strong practical performance. The contribution is a principled way to manage reliance on predictions, bringing worst-case protection in learning-augmented paging close to the best possible guarantee.
icml-2026-towards-optimal-robustness-in-.tldr: A relative prediction budget yields learning-augmented paging with optimal robustness up to an additive constant.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning can reuse data from a source domain when target-domain observations are scarce. However, differences in dynamics can make source transitions infeasible in the target, causing harmful transfer. ROOT addresses how to select usable source data when the amount of genuine overlap between domains is unknown.

The method learns soft weights for source samples so their geometry aligns with the target. A robust ambiguity set accounts for uncertainty from limited target observations. An unbalanced optimal transport objective then penalizes changes in transported mass, allowing the system to down-weight or discard costly matches rather than forcing all source data onto the target distribution.

The induced weights decrease exponentially with transport cost, providing a guarantee of outlier suppression. This gives the selection mechanism a principled response to poorly matching samples without task-specific threshold tuning. On D4RL benchmarks involving dynamics shifts, ROOT improves downstream offline reinforcement learning and outperforms strong baselines on most tasks. The findings support explicitly deciding what data to discard as part of cross-domain alignment.
icml-2026-transport-or-discard-robust-un.tldr: ROOT uses robust unbalanced optimal transport to retain useful source transitions and suppress mismatched data in cross-domain offline reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: A graph’s connections do not naturally fit the linear order of language-model tokens. Flattening a graph into a sequence can hide multi-hop relationships, while separate graph encoders can restrict token-level reasoning during generation. Weaver integrates graph structure directly into the attention mechanism of a decoder-only language model.

The framework treats context processing as message passing. It maps graph distances into rotary positional embeddings so structurally connected nodes become nearby in attention space. A masking mechanism accommodates causal tokens and graph structure, while Graph-over-Tokens RoPE jointly represents sequential position and graph distance. A local-information priority helps resolve positional ambiguity arising from graph symmetries.

On zero-shot benchmarks, Weaver reports state-of-the-art results among generative graph language models. Gains reach up to 30% over prior generative methods on heterophilic graphs, and performance matches specialized discriminative models on citation networks. These findings support encoding topology within decoder attention as a way to combine graph reasoning and language generation in one framework without a separate encoder.
icml-2026-weaving-graph-over-tokens-cont.tldr: Weaver embeds graph distances into decoder attention to support graph reasoning directly within a generative language model.
